c.tagline: Storied university city of grand colleges, riverside punting, and quiet cloistered courtyards.

taxi.fareNote: Traditional black cabs are metered and can be hailed on the street; minicabs should be pre-booked by phone or app.

emergency.note: 999 for emergencies; 101 for non-emergency police; 112 also reaches emergency services.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Bike theft is rife and pickpockets work the market square in summer; agree punting tour prices before boarding to avoid tout overcharging.

hood_desc: The historic university core packed with ancient colleges, King's College Chapel, the Fitzwilliam Museum, and the main shopping streets; almost everything a visitor wants is within walking distance.
A lively, multicultural strip of independent cafes, ethnic restaurants, and vintage shops just east of the centre, favoured by students and locals over tourists.
The scenic stretch of green lawns and gardens along the River Cam behind the historic colleges, best known for punting and classic photo views of the bridges and chapels.
A residential riverside district north of the centre with parks, meadows, and a relaxed, family-friendly feel along the Cam.
A leafy, affluent residential area southwest of the centre near the university's science and arts faculties, with the Newnham College grounds and quiet mill pool.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though notably hard.

transit.pay: Contactless card or phone tap, or Stagecoach smart ticketing app
transit.note: The city centre is compact and best explored on foot or by bike; Cambridge has one of the UK's highest cycling rates.

train: Direct trains to London King's Cross/Liverpool Street (~50 min)
bus: National Express coaches to London and major airports

tip.r: A 10-12.5% service charge is often added automatically at restaurants; round up for taxis and cafes if service was good.

food.name: Chelsea bun
food.desc: Sticky spiral of enriched dough with currants and citrus peel, glazed in syrup; a Cambridge student ritual for over a century.

places.name: Fitzbillies

landmarks: King's College Chapel
The pinnacle of English Perpendicular Gothic, its fan-vaulted ceiling, Tudor stained glass, and world-famous choir make this Cambridge's defining, most photographed silhouette.
Punting on the River Cam (The Backs)
Gliding by flat-bottomed punt past the manicured lawns and bridges behind the colleges is the quintessential Cambridge experience, best on a lazy summer afternoon.
Trinity College
Founded by Henry VIII and alma mater of Newton and Byron, its Great Court and Wren Library brim with treasures including Newton's own annotated Principia.
Fitzwilliam Museum
A neoclassical treasure house of Titians, Monets, Egyptian sarcophagi, and illuminated manuscripts, ranking among Britain's finest museums, with gloriously free admission.
Bridge of Sighs, St John's College
This romantic covered neo-Gothic bridge of 1831 arches over the Cam, a punt-perfect vista Queen Victoria reportedly loved above all else in Cambridge.
Mathematical Bridge, Queens' College
An ingenious 1749 timber bridge built from entirely straight beams that form an elegant arc, wrapped in the enduring myth that Newton designed it.
Great St Mary's Church
The university church since medieval times, whose 123-step tower delivers the classic rooftop panorama over King's Parade, market square, and college courts.
Corpus Clock and the Chronophage
A mesmerizing gold-plated clock devoured by a monstrous grasshopper 'time-eater', unveiled by Stephen Hawking and now one of Cambridge's quirkiest photo stops.
Cambridge University Botanic Garden
Forty heritage acres founded by Darwin's mentor John Henslow, where glasshouses, a winter garden, and 8,000 plant species offer year-round botanical theatre.
Round Church (Holy Sepulchre)
One of only four surviving medieval round churches in England, this thick-walled Norman gem of 1130 was inspired by Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre.

train.note: No international trains - change in London for Eurostar. Great Northern and Thameslink reach London King's Cross in about 50 minutes and Liverpool Street in 1h20, with Thameslink services running through to Gatwick and Brighton without changing in London, and CrossCountry trains north to Peterborough and Birmingham. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches. National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/) runs from Parkside to London Victoria in about 2h30 and, more usefully, direct to Stansted, Heathrow and Gatwick airports. The Busway guided bus links the city with St Ives and Huntingdon.

ferry.note: Cambridge is inland with no ferry. Punting on the Cam past the college Backs is the local boat tradition, hired by the hour rather than run to a timetable. The nearest international sailings are from Harwich, about two hours away, with Stena Line to Hook of Holland.

half.name: Ely
half.blurb: Fenland cathedral city dominated by its towering Norman cathedral, nicknamed the Ship of the Fens for its skyline.

half.name: London
half.blurb: British capital under an hour away by train, with its museums, palaces and West End theaters.

half.name: Bury St Edmunds
half.blurb: Market town built around the ruins of a once-powerful medieval abbey, with a Georgian theater and Regency-era gardens.

half.name: Duxford
half.blurb: Imperial War Museum airfield with historic aircraft hangars, a huge collection of vintage planes and a working WWII-era runway.
